THE OBJECT — one small single leaf of hand-drawn paper, a late-fifteenth-century Spanish horoscope figure, roughly 20 by 28 centimeters, drawn freehand by a working astrologer with a cut quill.

THE HANDWRITING — CRITICAL. Every mark on this page was made by a quill pen dipped in iron gall ink five hundred years ago, and it must look it. Nothing on this sheet is printed, typeset, or evenly inked.
Quill behaviour: the stroke swells thick and dark on every downstroke and thins to a fine hairline on every upstroke and connecting stroke, the width changing continuously within single letters. Ink pools and darkens where the nib paused, at the start of a stroke and at the foot of each descender. Small ink blots and spatter where the pen was set down hard.
Dipping rhythm: each dip starts dark and heavy, then the ink runs progressively drier across the next several words until the stroke breaks up into a scratchy dry-nib skip, and then the next dip goes dark again. This cycle repeats visibly all down the page, so the ink density varies from word to word and no two lines are the same weight.
Cursive, not print: joined-up secretary-hand cursive with a rightward slant, ascenders and descenders tangling between lines, letter shapes irregular and no two instances of the same letter identical, the baseline wandering slightly, spacing uneven, the ends of lines cramping as they run out of room.
Age in the ink: the iron gall has oxidised from black to warm rust-brown, unevenly — some strokes still dark brown, others faded to pale tan, several words almost lost where the ink went thin. The ink has bled slightly into the paper fibre so edges are soft and feathered rather than crisp. In two or three places the ink has bitten into the sheet and browned the paper around the stroke.
Legible but aged — the words can be read, but they read as five-hundred-year-old handwriting, not as clean modern lettering.

A large square ruled on the page, with straight lines drawn from corner to corner and from the midpoint of each side, dividing it into twelve triangular compartments around the edge and leaving a diamond-shaped space at the centre. SCENE CONTEXT
Daytime, 1520, inside a stone room in the Aztec palace the Spanish are occupying in the capital. An epic night battle inside a walled palace compound in a Mesoamerican city, 1520. The Spanish garrison is under mass assault and barely holding. Native Nahuatl warriors are swarming the compound from outside — scaling the high walls with ladders and ropes, hauling themselves over the parapet, fighting hand to hand along the top of the wall walk, and dropping down into the courtyard below to fight in the open ground among the timber, crates and horses. Spanish soldiers fight them on the walls, at the base of the walls, and in the yard. Light artillery on the wall top fires down into the massed attackers outside. The Spaniards are outnumbered many times over, exhausted and desperate, giving ground and taking it back, holding on by very little. It is chaotic, violent and close, and it happens almost entirely in darkness.

LOCATION
<<<image_1>>> — the compound: a high plastered wall painted with deep red geometric banding and painted roundels, a barred wooden gate, timber barricades, ladders leaning against the inner face of the wall, a walkway along the top, stone flagging and packed dirt underfoot, stacked cut timber, crates, coiled rope, picketed horses. This reference gives the place only. It does not set the time of day, the lighting, or any camera framing.

THE SPANISH
Every Spanish soldier wears a Spanish steel morion helmet. The morion is a single piece of hammered steel with a tall, sharp fore-and-aft comb running front to back over the crown like a low fin, standing roughly two fingers proud of the skull at its highest point. The brim is a single continuous piece that sweeps up sharply into a point at the front and again at the back, and dips down low over the ears at the sides, so the whole rim curves like the hull of a boat seen from above. There is no visor, no face plate and no cheek pieces — the face is completely open and the whole face is visible at all times. A row of small brass or iron rivets runs around the base of the brim. A leather chinstrap hangs loose or is tied under the jaw. The steel is dull, dark grey-brown, unpolished, pitted, scratched, dented from use and blotched with rust — these are not bright or shiny helmets. Some are plain, some have a slight roped edge to the brim, and they vary a little in comb height and brim sweep from man to man.
Under it, short-sleeved chain mail to mid-thigh over cream quilted cotton armor. Wide leather waist belts with a second slung belt, dark breeches to the knee with grey, brown, faded madder-red or off-white hose, tall folded-cuff leather boots or plain brown laced shoes. Everything frayed, sweat-stained, ground with dirt and crudely repaired — these men have been under siege for weeks and look starved and worn out. Long hair, unkempt beards, gaunt faces. No steel breastplates on anyone. They carry straight cross-hilt cut-and-thrust swords, long infantry spears, and round or kite shields. Bronze light cannon on wooden field carriages sit up on the wall walk. Every man dressed differently from every other man.

THE NATIVE NAHUATL WARRIORS
Adult Nahuatl men of central highland ancestry — lean and hard-muscled, deep brown skin, straight black hair, broad through the cheekbone with strong straight brows. Every one of them completely clean shaven, with no beard, no moustache, no stubble and no facial hair of any kind.

Their dress runs the full range from nothing to elaborate, and no two men are alike:
Many wear ichcahuipilli — sleeveless quilted cotton torso armor, thick as two fingers, layered unspun cotton stitched between cloth and bound at the edge with leather. It comes in several cuts across the crowd: some tie at the back, some lace at the front, some pull over the head and hug the body to the top of the thigh, some flare loose to mid-thigh. Painted in off-white, ochre, deep red and black, worn, stained and torn, some trimmed with rows of colored feathers.
Others fight bare-chested in nothing but a cotton loincloth wrapped between the legs and knotted at the front with the ends hanging.
Some wear short cotton capes knotted at one shoulder, one or two in bright red.
The senior fighters wear tlahuiztli — close-fitting full-body feathered war suits covering torso, arms and legs, opening at the back, in black and red, in green feather, in jaguar pelt with spotted hide, in eagle feather with a beaked headpiece. A few carry tall feathered back-banners rising off the shoulders on light frames. A few wear carved wooden helmets covering the skull and jaw.
Hair is worn many ways across the crowd: loose and long, bound in a knot on top of the head with a red cord, gathered into an upright column on the crown, cut short, or shaved.
Ornaments of bone, shell, greenstone and gold at the ears, nose and lip on some, none at all on others. Sandals with woven hide straps on some men, bare feet on others.

Paint appears on some of them and not on others. Where it appears it is specific and stark rather than decorative: some men painted black over the whole body with black stripes across the face, glittering with sprinkled mineral pyrite that catches the firelight; some with the face divided vertically, half blue and half red or yellow; some with the face washed in yellow and red. Most of the crowd wears no paint at all.

They carry macuahuitl — hardwood clubs about a metre long set with rows of black obsidian blades along both edges; long thrusting spears with obsidian-edged heads; bows; slings; and round shields of wood or woven cane, some plain, some faced with bright featherwork.

WHO IS WHO
Two sides, and they never fight their own. The Spanish are the men in steel morion helmets and mail over quilted cotton — they hold the walls and the yard and only ever fight native warriors. The native Nahuatl warriors are the clean-shaven men coming over the wall from outside — they only ever fight Spaniards. No Spaniard strikes another Spaniard at any point. No native warrior strikes another native warrior at any point.

THE FEEL
Overwhelming numbers against a thin, exhausted line. Warriors coming over the wall faster than they can be put down. Spaniards fighting shoulder to shoulder in small knots, giving ground and shoving forward again. Men falling off the wall walk into the yard. Bodies on the stone. Cannon firing down into the mass beyond the wall in flat concussive blasts. The warriors screaming raw frenzied war cries and throwing themselves forward with no regard for what happens to them; the Spaniards roaring with effort, working hard and frightened. Nobody is winning. The Spaniards are just barely holding.

Character reference sheet for film production. One 16:9 image divided into three
equal vertical panels against a seamless neutral light-gray studio backdrop. The
same man and the same garments appear in all three panels, identical in cut,
weave, color and wear. A costume turnaround for a historical drama.

ACTIVE REFERENCE
 — the man's face, age, build and hair. Identity and features 100% match
this reference.

SUBJECT
A Mexica man, central Mexico, year 1519, a prisoner being led through the city.
Middle-aged, lean and weathered, dark brown skin, tired and dust-streaked, a
scrape along one forearm. Long black hair loose past the shoulders, damp and
unkempt. Ears pierced, the ornaments gone. Bare feet, soles dark with dust.

RITUAL PREPARATION
His face, throat and hands are chalked white: a dry powdered lime wash, thin and
uneven, settling heavier in the lines of the face and thinning to bare skin over
the knuckles and the bridge of the nose. The dark skin reads through it in
patches, with streaks where sweat has cut channels down the temples and neck. The
chalk dusts the front lengths of his hair pale. No ornaments, no feathers, no
paper, no jewelry.

WARDROBE
Wrapped hip cloth of undyed maguey fiber, oatmeal cream, hand-loomed with a
coarse irregular weave, wound twice at the waist and falling to mid-thigh, the
woven ends hanging in front, edged with a narrow band of faded dark ochre, the
cloth soiled and dust-grayed.
Over it a tilmatli: a long rectangular mantle of coarse undyed maguey cloth,
pale grey-brown, draped over both shoulders and hanging closed down the front to
the knee, covering the chest and torso, the cloth stiff and creased, the hem
frayed. His arms are behind him beneath the mantle, the shoulders drawn back,
the cloth pulled taut across the upper chest by the set of his shoulders.
Pre-contact indigenous Mesoamerican only: hand-loomed plant fiber and natural dye.

PANEL 1 — LEFT
Full-length front view, the whole figure head to feet inside the frame, standing
upright, weight even on both feet, arms behind him, looking directly into the
lens with a still neutral expression. Face fully visible and sharp, the chalk
thin enough that the features read clearly: this is the identity reference.

PANEL 2 — CENTER
The same figure, same standing pose, rotated 45 degrees to his left so the camera
sees a three-quarter angle. Full length, head to feet in frame. Shows the fall of
the mantle down the side, the wrap of the hip cloth beneath it, and the set of
the shoulders.

PANEL 3 — RIGHT
The same figure, same standing pose, rotated to a rear three-quarter view. Full
length, head to feet in frame. Shows the spread of the mantle across the back,
the hair falling over it, the hands held low behind him with a length of coarse
maguey cord at the wrists, and the hem lengths from behind.

LIGHTING AND CAMERA
Even, soft, shadowless studio lighting, 5600K, front-and-side fill, faint contact
shadow under the feet only. Neutral 47 degree FOV, camera at chest height, no
perspective distortion, all three panels shot at the same distance and the same
scale so the figure's height matches across panels.

STYLE
Photorealistic, sharp fabric texture, visible individual weave threads and loose
fibers, chalk sitting as a dry powdered layer with visible grain, pore-level skin
detail, high resolution, flat product-reference lighting, plain background, no
props, no text, no labels.

An epic night battle inside a walled palace compound in a Mesoamerican city, 1520. The Spanish garrison is under mass assault and barely holding. Native Nahuatl warriors are swarming the compound from outside — scaling the high walls with ladders and ropes, hauling themselves over the parapet, fighting hand to hand along the top of the wall walk, and dropping down into the courtyard below to fight in the open ground among the timber, crates and horses. Spanish soldiers fight them on the walls, at the base of the walls, and in the yard. Light artillery on the wall top fires down into the massed attackers outside. The Spaniards are outnumbered many times over, exhausted and desperate, giving ground and taking it back, holding on by very little. It is chaotic, violent and close, and it happens almost entirely in darkness.

LOCATION
<<<image_1>>> — the compound: a high plastered wall painted with deep red geometric banding and painted roundels, a barred wooden gate, timber barricades, ladders leaning against the inner face of the wall, a walkway along the top, stone flagging and packed dirt underfoot, stacked cut timber, crates, coiled rope, picketed horses. This reference gives the place only. It does not set the time of day, the lighting, or any camera framing.

THE SPANISH HELMETS
Every Spanish soldier wears the classic Spanish comb morion — the iconic conquistador helmet, recognizable immediately by its silhouette.
The defining feature is the comb. It is a tall, thin, blade-like crest running front to back along the centre of the crown, standing four to five inches proud of the skull at its highest point — a high, sharp, prominent crest that dominates the shape of the helmet. It is a tall crest, not a low ridge, not a rounded bump, not a subtle raised line.
The brim is narrow and flat, sweeping up to a hard sharp point at the front and a matching hard sharp point at the back, and pinched in tight and low at the sides over the ears.
The helmet sits square and level on the head. It is never tilted, never pushed back off the brow, never worn at an angle.
The face is completely open — no visor, no face plate, no cheek pieces, no nasal bar. The whole face is visible at all times.
A row of brass rosette-headed rivets runs around the edge of the brim. A small socket sits at the back of the comb for a plume. A leather chin cord hangs loose or is tied under the jaw.
The steel is dull, dark grey-brown, unpolished, pitted, scratched, dented from use and blotched with rust. These are not bright, shiny, silver or parade helmets.
No other kind of helmet appears anywhere in this scene. No closed helms, no burgonets, no kettle hats, no sallets, no round helmets, no smooth domes, no fantasy helmets, no helmets with face protection of any kind.

THE SPANISH
Under the morion, short-sleeved chain mail to mid-thigh over cream quilted cotton armor. Wide leather waist belts with a second slung belt, dark breeches to the knee with grey, brown, faded madder-red or off-white hose, tall folded-cuff leather boots or plain brown laced shoes. Everything frayed, sweat-stained, ground with dirt and crudely repaired — these men have been under siege for weeks and look starved and worn out. Long hair, unkempt beards, gaunt faces. No steel breastplates on anyone. They carry straight cross-hilt cut-and-thrust swords, long infantry spears, and round or kite shields. Bronze light cannon on wooden field carriages sit up on the wall walk. Every man dressed differently from every other man.

THE NATIVE NAHUATL WARRIORS
Adult Nahuatl men of central highland ancestry — lean and hard-muscled, deep brown skin, straight black hair, broad through the cheekbone with strong straight brows. Every one of them completely clean shaven, with no beard, no moustache, no stubble and no facial hair of any kind.

Every single one of these men is fully dressed for war. Every one of them wears a substantial war garment covering the torso and hanging down past the hips to at least mid-thigh. Nobody is bare-chested. Nobody is stripped down. Nobody is in a loincloth, a breechcloth, a thong, or any minimal or revealing garment. There is no exposed midriff and no bare hips anywhere in this scene. These are armored soldiers of an army, dressed to fight, not tribal figures in scraps of cloth.

Most wear the ichcahuipilli — a heavy sleeveless quilted cotton war jacket, thick as two fingers, layered unspun cotton stitched between cloth and bound at the edge with leather, covering chest, back and stomach completely and hanging down past the hips to mid-thigh. It comes in several cuts across the crowd: some tie at the back, some lace at the front, some pull over the head, some flare loose at the hem. Painted off-white, ochre, deep red or black, worn, stained and torn, some trimmed with rows of colored feathers. Beneath the jacket, a broad woven cotton wrap covers the hips and upper legs.
Many also wear a rectangular woven cotton cloak knotted over one shoulder, in white, ochre, red or dark blue.
The senior fighters wear tlahuiztli — close-fitting full-body feathered war suits covering the torso and both arms to the wrist and both legs to the ankle, opening at the back, surfaced in tight overlapping feathers, in black and red, in green feather, in jaguar pelt with spotted hide, in eagle feather with a beaked headpiece. A few carry tall feathered back-banners rising off the shoulders on light frames. A few wear carved wooden helmets covering the skull and jaw.
Hair is worn many ways across the crowd: loose and long, bound in a knot on top of the head with a red cord, cut short at the jaw. Straight black hair lying flat against the head.
Ornaments of bone, shell, greenstone and gold at the ears, nose and lip on some, none at all on others. Sandals with woven hide straps laced up the ankle.

Paint appears on some of them and not on others. Where it appears it is specific and stark rather than decorative: some men painted black over the whole body with black stripes across the face, glittering with sprinkled mineral pyrite that catches the firelight; some with the face divided vertically, half blue and half red or yellow; some with the face washed in yellow and red. Most of the crowd wears no paint at all.

They carry macuahuitl — hardwood clubs about a metre long set with rows of black obsidian blades along both edges; long thrusting spears with obsidian-edged heads; bows; slings; and round shields of wood or woven cane, some plain, some faced with bright featherwork.

WHO IS WHO
Two sides, and they never fight their own. The Spanish are the men in comb morions and mail over quilted cotton — they hold the walls and the yard and only ever fight native warriors. The native Nahuatl warriors are the clean-shaven men coming over the wall from outside — they only ever fight Spaniards. No Spaniard strikes another Spaniard at any point. No native warrior strikes another native warrior at any point.

THE FEEL
Overwhelming numbers against a thin, exhausted line. Warriors coming over the wall faster than they can be put down. Spaniards fighting shoulder to shoulder in small knots, giving ground and shoving forward again. Spaniards climbing the ladders to get up onto the wall walk and fighting for the top of it. Men falling off the wall walk into the yard. Bodies on the stone. Cannon firing down into the mass beyond the wall in flat concussive blasts. The warriors screaming raw frenzied war cries and throwing themselves forward with no regard for what happens to them; the Spaniards roaring with effort, working hard and frightened. Nobody is winning. The Spaniards are just barely holding.

LIGHTING
Full night, long after dark. No daylight anywhere. The sky is near black with only the faintest trace of deep blue at the top.
This is a very dark, underexposed scene. Most of the frame is black or near black at all times. Large areas of every shot have no readable detail in them at all.
There are only a few fires in the whole compound — a small number of torches and one or two iron fire baskets, set far apart, with long stretches of complete darkness between them. Fires are sparse and small. Do not fill the space with light.
Light falls off very fast. A man two paces from a flame is half in shadow; a man four paces away is a silhouette; beyond that he is invisible. Faces in a medium shot are lit on one side only, with the other side lost to black. Bodies drop out of the light as they move and come back into it. Figures pass in and out of visibility.
Cannon fire throws a hard white flash for a fraction of a second, lighting a wide area once and then leaving it darker than before.
Steel catches small isolated highlights out of the darkness — the tall comb and swept brim of a morion picking up one hard line of light as a man turns. Shadows crush to true black with nothing recoverable in them.
Firelight burns warm at 2000K in small isolated pools against otherwise cold near-black surroundings. Nothing in the frame is evenly lit. Nothing is fully visible.

STYLE
Photorealistic historical war film, naturalistic and unstylized, real material texture on stone, plaster, steel, feather, cloth and skin. Fine organic film grain. Wide-format framing. Real weight and mass in every body and every impact.

AUDIO
No music. A wall of sound at maximum volume throughout — thousands of voices roaring at once, raw frenzied war cries close to the lens, Spanish soldiers shouting in overlapping indistinct Spanish, obsidian and steel on wood and shield, heavy body impacts, cannon fire, mail rattling, torches guttering, the screams of wounded and dying men, and a vast continuous roar from the city beyond the walls.

An epic night battle inside a walled palace compound in a Mesoamerican city, 1520. The Spanish garrison is under mass assault and barely holding. Mexica warriors are swarming the compound from outside — coming over the high walls on ladders and ropes, hauling themselves over the parapet, fighting hand to hand along the top of the wall walk, and dropping down into the courtyard below to fight in the open ground among the timber, crates and horses. Spanish soldiers fight them on the walls, at the base of the walls, and in the yard. The Spaniards are outnumbered many times over, exhausted and desperate, giving ground and taking it back, holding on by very little. The whole thing is seen from inside the fighting line, close enough to touch, and it happens almost entirely in darkness.

This reference gives the place only. It does not set the time of day, the lighting, or any camera framing. Flat hardwood paddle-blade about one metre long, roughly a hand's width across, with continuous rows of black obsidian blades set into grooved channels down both long edges, squared or slightly flared at the tip, wrapped hide or cord grip. Held one-handed by most men, two-handed by a few of the larger fighters. Swung in flat horizontal arcs and downward chops, never thrust like a sword.

Focus is pulled by hand, hunting slightly, sometimes landing late and catching up.

Handheld, operated at shoulder height inside the fighting line, one to two metres from the nearest man, on the shadow side. THE SPANISH
Every Spanish soldier wears a Spanish steel comb morion — the classic peaked comb morion. One piece of dull pitted grey-brown steel, a tall sharp comb running front to back over the crown like a raised ridge, the brim swept up to a distinct point at the front and a matching point at the back and pinched narrow at the sides, a line of brass rosette-headed rivets running around the brim edge, a small plume socket at the back, open face with no visor and no cheek pieces, worn cocked slightly back off the brow, chin cord under the jaw. Under it, short-sleeved chain mail to mid-thigh over cream quilted cotton armor. At this range the detail reads hard — sweat cutting tracks through grime, split lips, a broken rivet line in the mail, breath fogging in front of a face.

THE MEXICA WARRIORS — FACE AND BODY
Adult Nahua men of central Mexican highland ancestry — lean and hard-muscled, deep brown skin, straight black hair, broad through the cheekbone, wide-set dark eyes, strong straight brows, straight or slightly aquiline nose, full mouth. Every one of them completely clean shaven, with no beard, no moustache, no stubble and no facial hair of any kind. Every man a different face, height and build. Held this close, skin reads at pore level — sweat sheeting off shoulders, dust caked in the creases of the neck, the flush of effort under the skin, veins standing in the forearms.

THE MEXICA WARRIORS — RANK ACROSS THE CROWD
The mob reads as a real army with a visible ladder of rank, most of it made of ordinary men and only a few elites.

The bulk of them — commoner levies and young warriors. A maxtlatl loincloth of plain white cotton wrapped between the legs and knotted at the front with two decorated ends hanging down. Bare chested above it. Many with a plain white or ochre tilmatli cape knotted over one shoulder, one or two in bright red. Some barefoot, some in sandals of woven hide straps. They carry the plain wood-and-cane round shield, the bow, the sling, and simple fire-hardened clubs.

The proven fighters — ichcahuipilli, sleeveless quilted cotton torso armor two fingers thick, layered unspun cotton stitched between cloth and bound at the edge with leather. Several cuts across the crowd: some tie at the back, some lace at the front, some pull over the head and hug the body to the top of the thigh, some flare loose to mid-thigh. Painted off-white, ochre, deep red and black, worn, salt-stained and torn open in places, a few trimmed with rows of short colored feathers at the hem.

The veteran ranks — tlahuiztli, close-fitting full-body feathered war suits covering torso, arms and legs, laced closed up the back, the feathers laid in tight overlapping courses over a quilted base. Solid fields of black, deep red, yellow, or blue-green quetzal. A few of these men carry a tall light cane back-frame rising off the shoulders, dressed with long green quetzal plumes or a stepped fan of feathers, swaying hard as they move. A few wear carved wooden helmets shaped as a stylised animal head, covering the skull and jaw with the face looking out of the open mouth.

The two elite orders, only a handful of men in the whole crowd — cuāuhtli eagle warriors in tawny brown and white eagle-feather suits with a wooden helmet carved as an open eagle beak, the man's face inside it; and ocēlōtl jaguar warriors in tight spotted jaguar-pelt suits with the pelt head worn as a helmet, teeth around the brow. Their shields are faced with dense feather mosaic.

A very small number of cuāuhchicqueh shorn ones — head shaved bare except for a single long braid or upright tuft over the left ear bound with red cord, body and face painted, pushing out ahead of everyone else.

HAIR
Worn many ways across the crowd: loose and long to the shoulder; gathered up and bound into a stiff upright column of hair on the crown wrapped with a red or white cord, the veteran's warrior knot; a plain knot on top of the head; cut short at the jaw; shaved to the skin.

ORNAMENT
Ear spools of greenstone, shell or gold in stretched lobes; crescent nose plates of gold or bone; lip plugs of polished obsidian or greenstone below the mouth; shell and bone collars — on some men, and nothing at all on others.

PAINT
On some of them and not on others. Where it appears it is specific and stark rather than decorative: some men painted black over the whole body with black bands across the face, glittering with sprinkled mineral pyrite that catches the firelight; some with the face divided vertically, half blue and half red or yellow; some with the face washed in yellow and red; some with a single wide red stripe across the eyes. Most of the crowd wears no paint at all. At this range the paint shows its texture — laid on thick and cracking, smeared by sweat, running at the jaw.

The macuahuitl <<<42b4fdf1-9675-4f9f-b0f8-edc79452fe68>>>, in the hands of a large part of the crowd, swung in flat arcs that cross the lens. Tepoztopilli — long thrusting polearms with a broad flat wooden head edged on both sides with rows of obsidian blades, driven overhand past the shield rim. Atlatl spear-throwers with short fletched darts, launched from close behind the front rank. Bows with cane arrows. Slings whipped overhead and released. Round chimalli shields of wood or tight-woven cane, most plain, a few faced with bright feather mosaic in stepped-fret and crescent patterns, some with a hanging fringe of feathers or hide strips along the bottom edge.

The wall arrives as pieces: a ladder rung and a bare foot on it, knuckles cresting the parapet, a warrior's face coming up over the top edge of frame close enough to fill it, a Spaniard's boot stamping down on a gripping hand. Spaniards fight shoulder to shoulder in knots so tight the camera can barely find air between them, giving ground and shoving forward again, mouths open and roaring with effort, eyes moving fast and frightened. It comes in several cuts across the crowd: some tie at the back, some lace at the front, some pull over the head and hug the body to the top of the thigh, some flare loose to mid-thigh. Painted in off-white, ochre, deep red and black, worn, stained and torn, some trimmed with rows of colored feathers.
Others fight bare-chested in nothing but a cotton loincloth wrapped between the legs and knotted at the front with the ends hanging.
Some wear short cotton capes knotted at one shoulder, one or two in bright red.
The senior fighters wear tlahuiztli — close-fitting full-body feathered war suits covering torso, arms and legs, opening at the back, in black and red, in green feather, in jaguar pelt with spotted hide, in eagle feather with a beaked headpiece. A few carry tall feathered back-banners rising off the shoulders on light frames. A few wear carved wooden helmets covering the skull and jaw.
Hair is worn many ways across the crowd: loose and long, bound in a knot on top of the head with a red cord, gathered into an upright column on the crown, cut short, or shaved.
Ornaments of bone, shell, greenstone and gold at the ears, nose and lip on some, none at all on others. Sandals with woven hide straps on some men, bare feet on others.

Paint appears on some of them and not on others. Where it appears it is specific and stark rather than decorative: some men painted black over the whole body with black stripes across the face, glittering with sprinkled mineral pyrite that catches the firelight; some with the face divided vertically, half blue and half red or yellow; some with the face washed in yellow and red. Most of the crowd wears no paint at all.

They carry macuahuitl — hardwood clubs about a metre long set with rows of black obsidian blades along both edges; long thrusting spears with obsidian-edged heads; bows; slings; and round shields of wood or woven cane, some plain, some faced with bright featherwork.

WHO IS WHO
Two sides, and they never fight their own. The Spanish are the men in steel morion helmets and mail over quilted cotton — they hold the walls and the yard and only ever fight native warriors. The native Nahuatl warriors are the clean-shaven men coming over the wall from outside — they only ever fight Spaniards. No Spaniard strikes another Spaniard at any point. No native warrior strikes another native warrior at any point.

THE FEEL
Overwhelming numbers against a thin, exhausted line. Warriors coming over the wall faster than they can be put down. Spaniards fighting shoulder to shoulder in small knots, giving ground and shoving forward again. Men falling off the wall walk into the yard. Bodies on the stone. Cannon firing down into the mass beyond the wall in flat concussive blasts. The warriors screaming raw frenzied war cries and throwing themselves forward with no regard for what happens to them; the Spaniards roaring with effort, working hard and frightened. Nobody is winning. The Spaniards are just barely holding.

LIGHTING
Full night, long after dark. No daylight anywhere. The sky is near black with only the faintest trace of deep blue at the top.
This is a very dark, underexposed scene. Most of the frame is black or near black at all times. Large areas of every shot have no readable detail in them at all.
There are only a few fires in the whole compound — a small number of torches and one or two iron fire baskets, set far apart, with long stretches of complete darkness between them. Fires are sparse and small. Do not fill the space with light.
Light falls off very fast. A man two paces from a flame is half in shadow; a man four paces away is a silhouette; beyond that he is invisible. Faces in a medium shot are lit on one side only, with the other side lost to black. Bodies drop out of the light as they move and come back into it. Figures pass in and out of visibility.
Cannon fire throws a hard white flash for a fraction of a second, lighting a wide area once and then leaving it darker than before.
Steel and sweat catch small isolated highlights out of the darkness. Shadows crush to true black with nothing recoverable in them.
Firelight burns warm at 2000K in small isolated pools against otherwise cold near-black surroundings. Nothing in the frame is evenly lit. Nothing is fully visible.

STYLE
Photorealistic historical war film, naturalistic and unstylized, real material texture on stone, plaster, steel, feather, cloth and skin. Fine organic film grain. Wide-format framing. Real weight and mass in every body and every impact.

AUDIO
No music. A wall of sound at maximum volume throughout — thousands of voices roaring at once, raw frenzied war cries close to the lens, Spanish soldiers shouting in overlapping indistinct Spanish, obsidian and steel on wood and shield, heavy body impacts, cannon fire, mail rattling, torches guttering, the screams of wounded and dying men, and a vast continuous roar from the city beyond the walls.

LOCKS
No text of any kind anywhere in the frame.
Every Nahuatl warrior is completely clean shaven with no facial hair of any kind.
Every Nahuatl warrior is a different man — different face, height, build, hair, dress and weapon.
No Spaniard strikes another Spaniard and no native warrior strikes another native warrior.
Every figure in frame is an adult man.
The scene is very dark and underexposed, with most of the frame black or near black in every shot.
Fires are few, small and far apart, with large areas of complete darkness between them.
Light falls off sharply — figures move in and out of visibility and are often only partly visible or fully silhouetted.
No area of the frame is evenly or fully lit at any point.
No daylight anywhere in the frame.
One location, one time of night, one lighting setup throughout.

A massive timber rack: two enormous vertical posts of stripped, weathered wood, thicker than a man, set into a low stone platform, with a series of long horizontal crossbeams running between them at regular intervals from waist height to well above head height. Each crossbeam is a single heavy pole, warm golden-brown wood darkened with age and handling, the grain catching the light.

Threaded onto every crossbeam, packed tight side by side with no gaps, are human skulls — each pierced through both temples so the pole runs horizontally through the head, all facing outward toward the plaza in rows. THE GATEWAY (the focal point of the frame): a monumental Mexica gateway set in a high lime-plastered wall. The doors stand partly open with a gap between them. Above them an exposed timber lintel of stacked beams, rough-adzed. The jambs and the wall panels flanking the gate are covered in flat painted Mexica ornament: deep red and white step-fret bands, cross-and-flower motifs, interlocking geometric panels, a horizontal zigzag band running along the wall at chest height, and round painted plaques in blue, ochre and white set into the plaster like shields. The courtyard is immense and rectangular, extremely wide — about 120 meters across and 80
deep — with a huge expanse of open swept ground in the middle. It is floored in large
fitted dark basalt slabs worn smooth and grey-black. A covered colonnade runs down both
long sides on a very long repeating rhythm of square painted stone pillars carrying flat
wooden beam ceilings, the two colonnades set far apart on either side of the frame with a
great emptiness between them, the pillars shrinking into the distance. Walls are
cream-white lime stucco banded at waist height with a deep red ochre and turquoise-green
geometric step-fret frieze, with carved stone relief panels of a feathered serpent set into
the masonry. Flat roofs throughout, no arches anywhere.

The far wall stands three times a man's height, capped by a plain flat smooth parapet with
a clean level top edge and nothing piled on it. Centered in it is a wide rectangular
gateway under a massive squared stone lintel. The opening is blocked from the inside by a
single huge flat panel of heavy wooden slats, laid vertically and pegged to horizontal
crossbeams, pressed flat against the inner face of the wall and overlapping the stone jambs
and lintel generously all the way around, so the panel is visibly larger than the opening
it covers. Bracing it: three heavy bronze cannon on wooden carriages pushed muzzle-first
hard up against the face of the panel in a row, wheels chocked. Two long timber beams run
from near the top edge of the panel down at a steep angle into square sockets cut into the
basalt floor of the courtyard, wedged tight at their feet. The ground at the base of the
panel is bare, clean stone with nothing heaped against it. Flanking the gateway, older
doorways in the same wall are sealed solid with fresh pale plaster infill, obviously new,
whiter and slightly recessed against the weathered original stucco. A bare stone stair with
no railing climbs the wall to the roof.

Along the colonnade edges only, pushed well back out of the open ground: rows of straw
pallets and rolled blankets, stacked shields and long pikes leaning against the pillars,
sacks of grain, wooden barrels and crates, large ceramic water jars, banked cook fires
ringed in stone with iron pots, stacked stone shot. In the side ranges several rooms stand
open with their roof beams stripped out, leaving empty joist sockets in the wall tops. One
battered stone planter with a surviving agave is shoved against a wall, out of the way.

The center of the courtyard is completely bare, open, swept stone.

THE ROOM
Use the attached image as the reference for the architecture, materials and proportions — the same pale limestone walls in warm grey-cream plaster, the same painted stepped-fret banding as a wide frieze near the ceiling and a narrow double band at dado height in dark red and slate blue, the same heavy dark timber ceiling beams in close parallel courses, the same large pale limestone floor slabs with visible joints, the same recessed rectangular wall niches, the same low stone dais of two broad steps against the far wall with fret banding along its riser. Same scale, same restraint — a fine room, plain and severe.

CHANGES FROM THE REFERENCE
No doorway, no balcony opening, no view outside. The left wall is solid and unbroken, carrying the same plaster and painted banding across its full width. No chair, no throne, no seat of any kind. The dais is bare stone with woven reed mats laid across it.

THE GOLD BARS
Roughly two hundred crude hand-cast ingots — uneven edges, pitted and slightly misshapen from casting in open sand moulds, warm yellow, the cast surface rough but rubbed to a low sheen on the upper faces and along the edges where they have been handled and stacked. No stamps, no markings, no coins anywhere. Stacked in low tiers across the dais steps and along the base of the far wall, some stacks squared, others loose and leaning, a few bars fallen flat on the floor slabs where they slid off a pile. More gathered on reed mats spread across the floor.

AZTEC AND MIXTEC GOLDWORK
Lost-wax cast pieces, each one slightly different from its neighbours because each mould was broken to release it — no two identical. Warm gold that varies piece to piece from deep yellow to a coppery reddish cast, most of it burnished bright, some duller where the alloy shows through.
— Large cast pectorals worn on the chest, openwork, some in the form of feathered serpents with curling volutes and panaches, some as deity faces with rectangular openwork frames and small dangling bells along the lower edge.
— Ear spools and ear flares: broad hollow discs and flared tubes, some with fine drawn-wire filigree and granulation fused across the surface.
— Labrets: lip ornaments with a flat plate and a shaft, several with cast eagle and serpent heads.
— Cast bells in graduated sizes, hollow and pear-shaped with a slit mouth, strung in clusters.
— Necklaces of dozens of small hollow cast beads in the form of frogs, turtles and shells, each bead a fraction of an inch across.
— Thin hammered sheet-gold discs and perforated sheet ornaments, some crumpled at the edges, their curved surfaces catching the light in bright bands.
— Nose ornaments, finger rings, arm and leg bands.

JADE AND TURQUOISE
— Turquoise mosaic pieces: carved cedar wood cores completely covered in small tessellated turquoise tiles set in dark pine resin, with details picked out in red thorny oyster shell and white conch shell, and eyes inlaid with pyrite and shell. Include a double-headed serpent pectoral with an undulating body and a head at each end, and one or two mosaic masks. Surfaces finely fitted, slightly irregular, glossy where polished.
— Jade and greenstone: long multi-strand necklaces of polished round and tubular beads in mottled blue-green, apple green and grey-green, heaped in coils; large polished jade ear flares; small carved greenstone figures and beads; a carved jade mask.
— Gold pieces set with turquoise, jade-green stone, red shell and obsidian inlay.
— A few pieces in rock crystal, amethyst and obsidian, polished to a deep shine.

DISTRIBUTION
The room is full. Gold and jewelry occupy most of the floor, the dais and the steps, heaped in shallow woven baskets and wide low ceramic bowls that overflow, spilling onto the reed mats and the bare stone around them. Necklaces spill over basket rims and pool on the floor. A small gold pot sits in each wall niche. Open swept limestone floor remains only in the near foreground toward camera.

MATERIALS AND FINISH
Gold reads as soft heavy metal with a real burnish — polished enough to reflect, so curved and rounded surfaces carry bright travelling highlights and small pieces throw sharp specular points. Flat cast faces stay matte and porous by contrast, hammered surfaces show tool marks catching the light along their ridges, filigree and granulation glint as fine raised texture. Polished jade, turquoise and rock crystal pick up small hard highlights of their own. The mass of gold bounces a faint warm glow onto the pale plaster of the far wall and onto the underside of the dais step above it. Stones are polished but not faceted. Everything sits with real weight, the mats compressing under the stacks.

LIGHT
Warm daylight raking in low from a single high source off frame to the left, sweeping across the floor and up the far wall at a shallow angle so it skims the treasure rather than flooding it — a raking light that finds every curved and burnished surface and lights it up while the room falls into soft shadow at the edges and in the corners. The gold reads brightest along the edges of the piles where the beam crosses them, with hundreds of small bright points scattered through the heaped jewelry, falling away into warm shadow deeper in. Deep shadows with clean detail. Naturalistic and slightly underlit overall — the exposure of the reference image, with the gold carrying the brightness rather than the room.

CAMERA
Wide interior view at standing eye level, the room reading in full depth from the near floor to the far wall and dais. Neutral rectilinear lens, no distortion, deep focus with the whole room sharp.

Photorealistic architectural rendering. Naturalistic color, restrained contrast, fine natural grain. No people, no figures, no modern objects, no text. Real metal specularity, but no bloom, no glow, no lens flare, no glitter effect, no treasure-cave lighting. Maximum resolution, 16:9.

SCENE CONTEXT
Daytime, 1520, inside a stone room in the Aztec palace the Spanish are occupying in the capital. A single continuous take, shot over one officer's shoulder across the room toward the curtained doorway. Guerrero stands out in the middle of the room with his arms folded, facing away from the entrance. The man did not follow him in. Beltrán reaches back out through the curtain and hauls him bodily into the room. Guerrero, interrupted from behind, turns to see who is shouting at him. All dialogue is spoken in the Spanish of sixteenth-century Spain by men from Spain, with the soft lisped "th" on c and z.

1.5s to 3.0s — Behind Guerrero the curtain shifts and Beltrán bursts through at a sharp angle, shouldering past the folds so the cloth is only briefly opened and swings closed behind him. 3.0s to 8.0s — The appeal comes out of him in a rush from behind Guerrero — far too loud for the room, pitched high, words piling into each other, the first word repeated because he cannot get started cleanly. 8.0s to 11.0s — Beltrán holds the gesture, waiting. Nobody answers him. Guerrero remains as he is, unmoved, a man who has decided not to acknowledge this.
11.0s to 13.0s — A voice off frame, low and gravelled and contemptuous, asks who he is. Behind Guerrero, Beltrán turns and looks along his own outstretched arm to the curtain and finds the space beside him completely empty. His hand drops.
13.0s to 15.0s — Guerrero finally moves. Slowly and with visible reluctance he unweights and pivots on the spot toward the doorway behind him, arms staying folded across his chest the whole time. He does not square up to them and does not drop his arms — he turns just far enough to bring the entrance into his own eyeline, ending in three-quarter profile to camera. As he turns his body swings clear of the doorway and opens the view past him.
15.0s to 20.0s — Now unmasked, Beltrán wheels to the curtain, shoves his arm through the folds up to the shoulder, gets a fistful of sleeve and hauls, leaning his weight back into it. The Astrologer comes through the curtain — a tall man ducking his head slightly under the lintel, stepping in under his own power at his own unhurried pace, letting himself be pulled rather than resisting. He clears the cloth completely and walks fully into the room, coming to a stand beside Beltrán, both men entirely inside and both fully visible past Guerrero. The curtain falls closed behind him. 20.0s to 23.5s — Beltrán turns back to the commander, still gripping the sleeve, and the second line comes out cracking and high, pulling on the arm as he speaks. The Astrologer does not look up — his eyes stay down on the flagstones in front of him.

PERFORMANCE
Guerrero is a hard, exhausted commander who has just been told the only bridge out of the city is untested. He is not startled by the interruption and he does not hurry. The turn at 13.0s is reluctant and unimpressed — a man dealing with something beneath him, who keeps his arms folded to make the point. No alarm, no curiosity, no widening of the eyes. He gives it as little as possible.
Beltrán is in full panic, not approaching it. He has just committed a serious offence by bursting into a room of senior officers and he knows it, and he is doing it anyway because he believes he is going to die tonight. His voice is pitched high and thin, forced out too fast, breath audible under every word, climbing and breaking when he presses. He stumbles getting started, repeating the first word because his mouth is ahead of his thinking. Play the body at the same pitch: chest heaving with fast shallow breathing, weight rocking and never planted, hands flying out and back and gripping and dropping, a visible tremor in the fingers. He is in constant motion for the whole shot.
His panic has made him stupid — he genuinely did not notice the man he came to present was not behind him, and the discovery lands as the floor going out from under him, not as comedy.
The Astrologer is the exact opposite and holds that contrast throughout. Settled weight, slow even breathing, unhurried steps, no urgency at all. He does not resist being pulled and does not hurry. Once inside he keeps his eyes down on the floor and never looks up at the officers, at Beltrán, or at camera — deferential, uncomfortable, entirely without hope. He has already tried to tell these men once and been dismissed, and he is only here because somebody dragged him. He does not speak and does not react when Beltrán pulls at his sleeve.
